cards.title: Brand architecture: monolithic, endorsed, pluralistic
cards.summary: Choose how far the parent brand extends across product lines by picking a monolithic, endorsed or pluralistic architecture.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a new product line, category or sub-brand launches under the store's main name, an endorsed sub-name, or a standalone identity.
steps: Map where the store's revenue and recognition sit today: a monolithic architecture (e.g. FedEx) puts one master brand on everything, so every new SKU compounds one reputation.

An endorsed architecture keeps the parent visible but lets a sub-brand carry its own name; use it when the new line serves a different customer or price tier but you still want parent trust to transfer.

A pluralistic architecture (e.g. Yum Brands) lets brands stand alone; use it only when the sub-brand's audience genuinely wouldn't buy from the parent, since each identity costs its own marketing and design budget.
Pick per category, not per company: a store can run a monolithic core line and a pluralistic premium or niche line.
Before adding a sub-brand, ask whether the parent name would help or hurt conversion on the new PDP; if it would hurt, that argues for endorsed or pluralistic.
caveats: Each additional identity multiplies design and marketing overhead; the source frames architecture as a structural trade-off, not a free option.

cards.title: Naming categories: founder, descriptive, fabricated, metaphor, acronym, magic spell
cards.summary: Classify candidate brand or product-line names against six conventional naming patterns to judge fit and defensibility.
cards.use_when: Naming a new store, private-label line, product family or subscription program.
steps: Generate candidates deliberately across the six categories rather than from brainstorm alone: founder (named after a person), descriptive (states what it does), fabricated (invented word), metaphor (evokes an image), acronym (initials-based), magic spell (evocative sound with no literal meaning).

Score each candidate on two axes: how quickly a new shopper understands the category (descriptive and founder names are fastest) and how legally and linguistically defensible it is (fabricated and magic-spell names are easiest to own).
Use descriptive names for search discovery of a straightforward line; use fabricated or magic-spell names for a line you intend to trademark and extend.
Acronym names only work once the underlying phrase is already known, so treat them as a scaling risk for a new brand.
Check the name survives as a handle, domain and spoken word before committing.
caveats: The source supplies the categories as a structural framework, not trademark advice; run actual clearance before launch.

cards.title: Tagline structures: imperative, descriptive, superlative, provocative, specific
cards.summary: Pick a tagline type by the job it must do on the PDP, homepage or ad, rather than by taste.
cards.use_when: Writing or replacing a store tagline, hero headline, packaging line or ad slogan.
steps: Identify the job: imperative tells the shopper to act; descriptive states what the brand or product is; superlative claims best-in-class; provocative unsettles to earn attention; specific names a concrete attribute, number or use.

Match the type to the awareness stage: descriptive and specific work for cold traffic that doesn't know the category; imperative suits a known offer ready to convert; superlative and provocative suit crowded categories where differentiation, not clarity, is the bottleneck.
Keep the tagline distinct from the brandmark; it should carry meaning the visual mark cannot.
Test by removing the product image: if the line alone doesn't communicate the category or the claim, it is too vague for a landing page.
caveats: Superlative claims invite substantiation and compliance problems; verify any 'best' or '#1' claim before publishing.

cards.title: Sequence of cognition: shape, then color, then form
cards.summary: Design marks so customers recognise the store first by silhouette, then by colour, and only then by detailed form.
cards.use_when: Designing or auditing a logo, app icon, packaging or ad thumbnail for recognition at small sizes and in feeds.
steps: Follow the source's sequence of visual cognition: shape is processed first, colour second, form (lettering and detail) last.
Build the mark so its distinctive shape reads in a one-colour, tiny rendition — favicon, app icon, social avatar, thumbnail.
Then make the colour ownable and consistent across packaging, ads and site so it becomes the second recognition cue.
Treat wordmark and letterform detail as the last layer, not the first; if legibility of the name is the only recognition cue, the mark fails at speed and small size.
Audit by blurring or reducing the mark to test whether shape and colour alone identify the store.
caveats: The source presents this as the order of visual processing, not a rule that form is unimportant; all three layers still matter.

cards.title: Brandmark typologies and dynamic marks
cards.summary: Choose among wordmarks, letterforms, pictorial, abstract, emblems, dynamic marks and characters based on what the brand must communicate.
cards.use_when: Commissioning or choosing a logo type for a new store, private label or rebrand.
steps: Wordmark: the name set in distinctive type — strongest when the name itself is short and memorable.
Letterform: initials only — compact and useful at small sizes, but depends on the name already being known.
Pictorial: a literal image of what the brand sells — fast category recognition, weaker differentiation.
Abstract: a non-literal symbol — most ownable but needs time and spend to acquire meaning.
Emblem: text locked inside a shape — reads as a badge or seal, good for packaging and heritage cues.
Character or dynamic mark: a mascot or a mark that changes across contexts; the source treats dynamic marks as a growth-stage option for brands that need variety across campaigns and seasons.
Match the typology to the store's recognition budget: unknown brands usually need pictorial or descriptive support; established brands can afford abstract.
caveats: Abstract marks carry no meaning until marketing invests in them; don't choose one expecting instant comprehension.

cards.title: Brand Ideals framework: nine tests for identity decisions
cards.summary: Screen brand and range decisions against nine ideals — vision, meaning, authenticity, coherence, flexibility, commitment, value, differentiation, sustainability.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a rebrand, a new product line, a packaging system or a brand partnership before committing budget.
steps: Vision: does the identity express a clear intended future, not just the current catalogue?
Meaning: does it signify something to the customer beyond the product?
Authenticity: is the claim supported by what the store actually does — sourcing, service, returns?
Coherence: do the site, packaging, ads and tone hold together as one system?
Flexibility: can it stretch across new categories, channels and languages without breaking?
Commitment: is the organisation prepared to sustain it over years, not one campaign cycle?
Value: does it add economic value (pricing power, recall, loyalty) rather than just looking better?
Differentiation: does it separate the store from competitors a shopper would otherwise consider?
Sustainability: can it be maintained operationally and ethically long term?
Use it as a checklist: score the proposal on all nine and treat any weak ideal as a reason to revise, not to reject automatically.
caveats: The source gives these as ideals to weigh, not a weighted scoring model; don't invent numeric thresholds.

cards.title: Cross-cultural identity translation for global selling
cards.summary: Separate objective, subjective and cultural variables when adapting a store identity, packaging or campaign to another market.
cards.use_when: Localising a storefront, packaging, imagery or campaign for a new country or language market.
steps: Split the identity into objective variables (legible facts: name, product, price, function), subjective variables (taste, colour preference, aesthetic judgement) and cultural variables (symbols, taboos, humour, ritual meaning).
Keep objective elements fixed so the brand stays recognisable; adapt subjective and cultural elements.
Audit colour, animal and gesture symbolism per market before reusing campaign imagery — a visual that reads as premium in one market can read as a warning or an insult in another.
Check the name itself for unintended meaning and transliteration problems before launch.
Decide whether the mark stays monolithic across markets or takes a local variant, and record that decision so regional teams don't improvise.
caveats: The source frames this as identity translation, not a full localisation playbook; verify market-specific claims locally.

cards.title: Map customer experience as a distinct economic offering
cards.summary: Treat the designed experience, not just the product, as the thing customers pay for, and build it from mapped touchpoints.
cards.use_when: Designing or overhauling the end-to-end store journey — from first ad impression through delivery, unboxing, support and repeat purchase.
steps: List every touchpoint in chronological order, from the first sighting of the brand (an ad, a search result, a shelf) to post-purchase support and returns, as the source does for a hotel (seeing it from the highway, entering the lobby, glimpsing the room).
Mark each touchpoint as functional (must work) or experiential (shapes memory and willingness to pay a premium).

Apply the five principles of experience design: make it ubiquitous (available across contexts), social (shared with or influenced by others), semantic (carries meaning), sentient (responsive to the customer's state or data) and human (feels like a person, not a system).
Use the map to find gaps — e.g. an excellent PDP followed by a generic shipping email undermines the paid-for experience.
Choose which two or three touchpoints deserve disproportionate investment rather than spreading budget evenly.
caveats: The five-principle framing is the source's own; treat it as a design lens, not a proven conversion model.

cards.title: Identify moments of truth in the purchase journey
cards.summary: Find the specific instants that determine whether the customer keeps or abandons the brand, and engineer those first.
cards.use_when: Prioritising which page, email, packaging element or support interaction to fix next when resources are limited.
steps: Walk the journey chronologically and name the decisive instants, as the source does for a hotel: seeing the property from the highway, walking into the lobby, glimpsing the room.
Translate that pattern to ecommerce: the search result or ad impression, the first fold of the PDP, the cart and checkout, the delivery notification, the unboxing, and the first support contact.
For each moment of truth, define what the customer is deciding (is this the right product; can I trust this store; did I get value) and what evidence resolves it.
Concentrate redesign effort on moments the customer cannot skip; secondary pages get less return.
Re-map after any major change to traffic source or offer, since the decisive moment can move.
caveats: The hotel example is the source's; the ecommerce sequence is an adaptation, not a demonstrated result.

cards.title: Five-step organic social strategy
cards.summary: Build organic social as objective, community, content, management and measurement — not as an unplanned posting habit.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restructuring the store's organic social channels to support brand and retention rather than only paid acquisition.
steps: Objective: state what the channel is for (awareness, community, support deflection, repeat purchase) before producing content.
Community building: decide whose conversations you are joining or hosting, and how you will respond to them consistently.
Content: plan formats and themes against the objective rather than reacting to trends.
Management: assign who posts, who answers comments and who escalates, and set a cadence.
Measurement: evaluate qualitatively as well as numerically — the source warns against vanity metrics without an assessment framework.
Keep paid social and ad creative in a separate plan; the source treats organic strategy and paid acquisition as distinct activities.
caveats: The source treats organic community building as mostly baseline practice with advanced community work as the minority of effort.

cards.title: Disclosure best practices for brand social accounts
cards.summary: Apply over-disclosure and anti-loophole rules so branded posts meet disclosure expectations.
cards.use_when: Publishing sponsored content, affiliate links, gifted-product posts or employee advocacy from the brand account.
steps: Adopt an over-disclosure stance: make the commercial relationship visible where a reader would encounter it, rather than burying it in hashtags or bios.
Close common loopholes: disclosure in a linked page, a personal profile rather than the post, or an ambiguous tag all fail the intent of disclosure.
Standardise a disclosure format and required placement for the store's own posts, creator partnerships and affiliate activity.
Train anyone posting on the brand's behalf on the rule, and include it in creator briefs.
Review disclosure practice when platforms change their tools or labels; verify the current platform interface before relying on a built-in label alone.
caveats: The source gives general best practice; disclosure requirements vary by jurisdiction and platform and should be checked against current rules.

cards.title: Crisis communications checklist for brand social channels
cards.summary: Prepare a proactive crisis plan — predetermined triggers, 24/7 monitoring, aligned messaging and a rule against deleting criticism.
cards.use_when: Writing the store's social crisis plan, or responding to a viral complaint, product-safety issue or fulfilment failure.
steps: Establish organisational protocols that define in advance what counts as a crisis and who declares it, so escalation isn't debated mid-incident.
Set up 24/7 social monitoring schedules, since incidents on social channels don't keep business hours.
Prepare key messages and align them across the team before responding publicly, so different accounts don't contradict each other.
Stand up a dedicated microsite or status page where customers can get authoritative updates.
Adopt transparent engagement protocols and follow the source's rule: do not delete negative comments — removal typically amplifies the incident and forfeits credibility.
Respond in public where the criticism was public, and move detailed resolution to a private channel.
caveats: The source presents this as proactive planning guidance, not a guarantee of incident outcomes; local legal and PR advice may override specific steps.

cards.title: Personal branding as 'Me Inc.' for founders and store owners
cards.summary: Manage the owner's or founder's public reputation as a brand asset with the same discipline as the company brand.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much the founder's name and persona should carry in the store's marketing, packaging and social presence.
steps: Treat the person as a managed identity — the source's 'Me Inc.' — with a defined positioning rather than an ad hoc posting pattern.
Decide deliberately whether the founder's identity should sit inside the store brand (helps trust and differentiation for small brands) or separate from it (limits reputational spillover).
Keep the personal channel's claims consistent with what the store actually delivers; a mismatch undermines the commercial brand.
Apply the same crisis discipline to the personal channel as to the brand account, since the two reputations transfer.
caveats: The source treats personal branding as reputation management, not a growth tactic; don't assume founder visibility improves conversion.

04-BRD / brand Goes here. The structural and strategic foundations of brand identity. Covers brand architecture models (monolithic, endorsed, pluralistic), naming conventions (founder, descriptive, fabricated, metaphor, acronym, magic spell), tagline categories (imperative, descriptive, superlative, provocative, specific), and brandmark typologies (wordmarks, letterforms, pictorial, abstract, emblems, dynamic marks, characters). Also includes the "Brand Ideals" framework (vision, meaning, authenticity, coherence, flexibility, commitment, value, differentiation, sustainability) and cross-cultural identity translation. Not here. • Mapping specific customer touchpoints and moments of truth -> 17-CXP • Community management and organic social media policies -> 13-ORG • Package engineering and raw materials sourcing -> 18-COG

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Codifies the exact architectural structures of brand identity, defining specific trademark categories, naming conventions, and brand architecture models (monolithic vs. pluralistic). modules: [BRD] topics: [brand architecture, naming conventions, taglines, brandmarks, brand ideals, cross-cultural branding] tier: 1 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. brand architecture / monolithic, endorsed, and pluralistic frameworks; naming / founder, descriptive, fabricated, metaphor, acronym, and magic spell categories; taglines / imperative, descriptive, superlative, provocative, and specific structures; brandmarks / sequence of cognition (shape, color, form), wordmarks, letterforms, pictorial, abstract, emblems, dynamic, and character marks; brand ideals / vision, meaning, authenticity, coherence, flexibility, commitment, value, differentiation, sustainability; cross-cultural / objective, subjective, and cultural variables in global brand adaptation. Look for. Distinct categorizations of brand architecture (e.g., Monolithic = FedEx; Pluralistic = Yum Brands). The sequence of visual cognition (shape -> color -> form) validating visual processing speed. Specific classifications of taglines and names. Explicit definitions of brand ideals. Skip. Vague platitudes about "design is good business." General history of specific logos unless providing a structural framework. Scope mix. 80% baseline (the foundational definitions of brand marks, names, and architecture), 20% growth (dynamic marks, private labeling strategy, brand licensing). Volume. 500 to 700 words.

17-CXP / post-purchase and experience Goes here. Designing the brand experience as a distinct economic offering. Identifying and curating customer touchpoints, mapping "moments of truth," and applying the five principles of experience design (ubiquitous, social, semantic, sentient, human). Not here. • Visual identity design, logo files, and typography standards -> 04-BRD • Developing the responsive grid for web or mobile apps -> 07-LPG

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Defines the customer experience as a distinct economic offering, outlining the specific transition from touchpoint identification to moment-of-truth optimization. modules: [CXP] topics: [customer experience, touchpoints, moments of truth, interactive branding] tier: 2 scope_hint: growth

Topics. customer experience / touchpoint mapping, moments of truth, experience as a distinct economic offering; design principles / ubiquitous, social, semantic, sentient, and human. Look for. Definitions of specific touchpoints and the chronological mapping of the "moment of truth" (e.g., sighting the hotel from the highway -> walking into the front lobby -> glimpsing into the room). Skip. General praise for basic customer service or vague assertions about "delighting the customer" without a structural framework. Scope mix. 40% baseline (identifying touchpoints), 60% growth (engineering sentient/semantic brand experiences). Volume. 200 to 300 words.

13-ORG / organic and social Goes here.
